In 1982, my husband, Frank, designed a cockpit alert system that warned pilots when the plane’s wings were icing up. Before it existed, ice had caused several crashes. Frank never talked about it as anything more than “one of my projects.” He came home that year, kissed me and said the company had given him “a nice settlement and some free flights.” That was all.

The settlement, the director explained, included a small royalty on every system installed across the airline’s fleet, payable to Frank and his heirs, and a lifetime travel pass that never expired. The royalties had been paid into a trust account for nine years since Frank’s death because the company had our old address.

The young lounge employee who had called security was asked to apologize, and she did, with tears in her eyes. She said she’d never seen a pass that old. I told her that was because the man who’d earned it had never once bragged about it.

The elderly employee who had recognized Frank’s name was named Joe. He’d been a junior mechanic when Frank trained him in 1983. “He taught me to check everything twice,” Joe said. “I’ve been doing it for forty years.”

The airline flew me to Chicago in first class and sent a car to the wedding. My granddaughter, Sarah, cried when I told her the story during the reception. She asked her new husband to raise a glass “to Grandpa Frank, who kept planes safe and never told anyone.”

The royalty money paid for Sarah’s wedding gift and for scholarships at the engineering school Frank attended. I still carry the same leather suitcase. Joe always meets me at the gate when I fly through his airport.
